L112: ## Relationships
L113: 
L114: We maintain an expansive set of relationship types to support the various content items that a research object, like a journal article, might link to. For data and software, we ask you to provide the following information:
L115:   * identifier of the dataset/software
L116:   * identifier type: DOI, Accession, PURL, ARK, URI, Other (additional identifier types are also accepted beyond those used for data or software, including ARXIV, ECLI, Handle, ISSN, ISBN, PMID, PMCID, and UUID)
L117:   * relationship type: isSupplementedBy or references (use the former if it was generated as part of the research results)
L118:   * description of dataset or software
L119: We and cite58†DataCite†datacite.org both use this kind of linking. Data repositories which register their content with DataCite follow the same process and apply the same metadata tags. This means that we achieve direct data interoperability with links in the reverse direction (data and software repositories to journal articles).
L120: 
L121: You can see illustrations and examples of this schema in our cite59†data and software citation guide .
L122: ### Declaring relationship types
L123: 
L124: The possible relationship types between content items can be as varied as the items themselves. We use a controlled vocabulary to define these relationships, in order to construct an orderly mapped network of content.
L125: This is achieved by (i) an implicit approach where the relation type is a function of a specific service and is declared in the structure of the deposited XML, and (ii) in an explicit approach where the relation type is selected as a value within the deposited metadata.
L126:   1. cite60†Reference linking and cite37†Cited-by : implicitly creates `cites` and `isCitedBy` relationships between a content item and the items in its bibliography
L127:   2. cite36†Crossmark : explicit creation of cite61†update relations†data.crossref.org between an item and other items that materially affect it (for example, a retraction)
L128:   3. cite62†Funding data : implicit creation of `isFundedBy` and `hasAward` relationships between an item and the funding source that supported the underlying research
L129:   4. Linked clinical trials: implicit creation of a `belongsTo` relationship between and item and a registered clinical trial
L130:   5. cite63†Components : implicit creation of a `isChildOf` relationship between an item and its elemental parts that are assigned their own DOI (limited cite64†parent relation typing†data.crossref.org )
L131:   6. General typed relations: explicitly typed relation between an item with a Crossref DOI and an item with one of several possible identifiers.

L113: ## Posted content (includes preprints) markup guide
L114: 
L115: This guide gives markup examples for members registering posted content (includes preprints) by direct deposit of XML. It is not currently possible to register the posted content (includes preprints) record type using one of our helper tools.
L116: ## Depositing and updating posted content
L117: 
L118: Posted content is a Crossref record type available starting with cite34†schema version 4.4.0. The schema updates include a number of posted content-specific elements. The top level element is called `posted_content` and has an attribute called `type`. This attribute is given a value from an enumerated list that defines the nature of the posted content. The current set of enumerations are:
L119: 
L120:   * preprint
L121:   * letter
L122:   * other
L123:   * blog
L124:   * poster
L125: Please cite58†contact us†support.crossref.org if you want to deposit metadata for a posted record type which is not on this list.
L126: ## Metadata elements
L127: 
L128: The posted record type contains the following elements (* = required ** available as of schema version 5.4.0):
L129: Element  | Description
L130: --- | ---
L131: `group_title`  | The hosting platform may organize its posted content into categories or subject areas. This field is used to name the container for the posted item
L132: `contributors`  | Container for author information
L133: `titles`*  | The titles (title and subtitle) of the posted content
L134: `posted_date`*  | The date when the posted content became available online on the hosting platform
L135: `acceptance_date`  | The date the content item was submitted to and accepted by the hosting platform
L136: `institution`  | Container for information about an organization that sponsored or hosted an item, such as a repository or preprint server
L137: `institution_name`  | name of an organization that sponsored or hosted an item
L138: `institution_id`  | PID of the sponsoring or hosting institution (supported values are `ror, wikidata, isni`)
L139: `status`**``  | status of preprint (`withdrawn` or `removed`)
L140: `version_info, version, description`**``  | version number and description of version changes
L141: `program: funding`  | Source of funding applicable to research related to the posted content
L142: `program: access indicators`  | License terms
L143: `program: relations`  | Relationships (other than bibliographic citation) to other works, such as found in acknowledgments or list of supplemental material
L144: `doi_data`*  | Container for persistent identifier and URL
L145: `citation_list`  | Posted content bibliography listing of citations to other works

L113: ## Introduction to posted content (includes preprints)
L114: ### Why register posted content
L115: 
L116: Posted content includes preprints, eprints, and other types of content that have been posted to a stewarded host platform. We’re all about persistence, so it’s vital that everything registered with us be maintained. Note that accepted manuscripts are not considered posted content.
L117: A preprint should remain online once it has been posted, including once it has appeared in a journal or if an updated version becomes available. If different versions become available, the preprint owner should update the preprint metadata using cite58†relations tags . In exceptional cases where a preprint is removed, such as in the case of plagiarism or other misconduct, we recommend that the DOI resolves to a page containing at least the title, authors, and a short explanation of the removal.
L118: Preprint owners should refer to good practice for journal article retraction in this case. Note that we cannot remove preprint metadata from our records.
L119: ## Publishing preprints is about more than simply getting a DOI
L120: 
L121: Crossref can help you to clearly label content as a preprint using a preprint-specific schema. It’s not advisable to register preprints as data, components, articles, or anything else, because a preprint is not any of those things. Our service allows you to ensure the relationships between preprints and any eventual article are asserted in the metadata, and accurately readable by both humans and machines.
L122: ## Benefits of our custom support for preprints
L123:   * Persistent identifiers for preprints to ensure successful links to the scholarly record over the course of time
L124:   * The preprint-specific metadata we ask for reflects researcher workflows from preprint to formal publication
L125:   * Support for preprint versioning by providing relationships between metadata for different iterations of the same document.
L126:   * Notification of links between preprints and formal publications that may follow (such as journal articles, monographs)
L127:   * cite59†Reference linking for preprints, connecting up the scholarly record to associated literature
L128:   * cite60†Auto-update of ORCID records to ensure that preprint contributors are acknowledged for their work
L129:   * Preprints cite61†include funding data†doi.org so people can report research contributions based on funder and grant identification
L130:   * Discoverability: we make the metadata available for machine and human access, across multiple interfaces (including our cite62†REST API , cite63†OAI-PMH , and cite64†Metadata Search†search.crossref.org .

L111: ## Discovering relationships between preprints and journal articles
L112: 
L113: cite60†Image: Dominika Tkaczyk L114: 
L115: cite61†Dominika Tkaczyk – 2023 December 07
L116: 
L117: In cite62†Preprints cite63†Linking cite64†Metadata Matching L118: In the scholarly communications environment, the evolution of a journal article can be traced by the relationships it has with its preprints. Those preprint–journal article relationships are an important component of cite31†the research nexus . Some of those relationships are provided by Crossref members (including publishers, universities, research groups, funders, etc.) when they deposit metadata with Crossref, but we know that a significant number of them are missing.
L119: To fill this gap, we developed a new automated strategy for discovering relationships between preprints and journal articles and applied it to all the preprints in the Crossref database. We made the resulting dataset, containing both publisher-asserted and automatically discovered relationships, cite65†publicly available†doi.org for anyone to analyse.
L120: ## TL;DR
L121: 
L122:   * We have developed a new, heuristic-based strategy for matching journal articles to their preprints. It achieved the following results on the evaluation dataset: precision 0.99, recall 0.95, F0.5 0.98. The code is available cite66†here†gitlab.com .
L123: 
L124:   * We applied the strategy to all the preprints in the Crossref database. It discovered 627K preprint–journal article relationships.
L125:   * We gathered all preprint–journal article relationships deposited by Crossref members, merged them with those discovered by the new strategy, and made everything available as cite65†a dataset†doi.org . There are 642K relationships in the dataset, including:
L126:     * 296K provided by the publisher and discovered by the strategy,
L127:     * 331K new relationships discovered by the strategy only,
L128:     * 15K provided by the publisher only.
L129:   * In the future, we plan to replace our current matching strategy with the new one and make all discovered relationships available through the Crossref REST API.

L112: ## Tips and tricks
L113: 
L114: We love to share our data and we want it to be used. Yes, really—and by as many people as possible. Here we share tips to help you get the most out of our REST API. Everyone benefits if you use our REST API responsibly and efficiently. Very occasionally we have had to block users who misuse our APIs, usually through carelessness rather than malice. If you follow the advice on this page you should have no problem.
L115: Note that for conciseness, the examples on this page omit the API URL, which is cite58†https://api.crossref.org/v1†api.crossref.org , so for an example like `/members/120` the full query is cite59†https://api.crossref.org/v1/members/120†api.crossref.org .

Rows and cursors L123:   * cite65†Large numbers of queries and very large results sets L124:   * cite66†How to keep your local data synced with the REST API L125:   * cite67†Code Libraries L126: ### Where do I start?
L127: 
L128: If you are just getting started with our API, we recommend heading to the cite68†API Learning Hub . There you can get to grips with APIs, what kind of metadata you can retrieve, and how to formulate queries. For a description of the endpoints and request parameters, see our cite69†Swagger documentation†api.crossref.org , where you can try out some queries.
L129: ### Get the right endpoint
L130: 
L131: Most of our queries go through the `/works` endpoint. If you’re looking for research outputs such as journal articles, that’s probably where you want to start.
L132: Bear in mind that we also have cite70†other endpoints , including `/prefixes`, `/journals`, and `/members`. You can, for example, get all works in a journal by using its ISSN, e.g.: `/journals/0003-3804/works`. The members endpoint contains summary metadata about organisations that have deposited metadata, including which metadata fields they deposit and the fraction of records with certain properties e.g.: `/members/120`.
L133: ### Use filter and query parameters
L134: 
L135: Our API contains a range of parameters that can be used to pull out records that match certain criteria. For example, various kinds of date filters: `/works?filter=from-pub-date:2024-01-01,until-pub-date:2025-12-31` will get all records with a publication date in 2024.
L136: There are filters to detect the presence of certain properties, e.g., `/works?filter=has-references:1,filter=has-orcid:1` will return only works with both references and authors where at least one has an ORCID ID.
L137: 
L138: There are also filters for specific values, e.g., `/works?filter=type:journal-article,funder:10.13039/100000040` retrieves journal articles funded by the organisation with the specified funder ID.
L139: If you are looking to analyse a large number of metadata records, such as all records from a single journal or publisher, it is almost always more efficient to query using a filter than for each DOI individually.
L140: ### Be selective with fields, if you need to be
L141: 
L142: If you are only interested in a few fields of the output from the works endpoint, you can use `select` to retrieve only that metadata. For example, `/works?rows=10&select=DOI` returns the DOI field. This can make your API calls much more efficient. For example:
L143: 
L144:   * Retrieve 10 random DOIs in the Crossref corpus with only the DOI and record title: `https://api.crossref.org/works?sample=10&select=DOI,title`
L145:   * Retrieve all works for ISSN 1527-2095 with only these elements returned in the results: DOI, title, and page number (only the first 20 results are returned): `https://api.crossref.org/journals/1527-2095/works?select=DOI,title,page`
L146: ### How much metadata? Rows and cursors
L147: You can make more efficient use of the API and get results more quickly by thinking in advance about how many results you need. The default number of rows returned is 20 and you can increase it up to 1000. If you have a query where you only need to know the total number of results, you can use `rows=0`. For requests with a query parameter, 2–5 rows might be enough (see more on that below), whereas to look at a few examples of records with a certain property, maybe 10 records is enough.
